topics.title: Design for a very small working memory
topics.theory: Memory architecture: three stores, about four chunks

situation.text: You have a lot to cover and a room of people who are new to it. The easy move is to put everything on the slides and keep going.

items: Choose the few ideas people must leave with. Three or four, not ten.
Introduce them one at a time. Let people use each one before you add the next.
Group related details under one idea, so they travel together.
Move anything people can look up later off the slide and into a handout.

why.text: Working memory is where people hold new information while they think about it. It is small: about three to five things at once, and fewer when the material is unfamiliar.

Past that limit people start dropping items, and what is dropped is not learned. Once ideas are grouped and practised they move into long-term memory, which frees the space again. Experts seem to hold more because their chunks are bigger.

why.caption: New information has to pass through a small working memory before it can settle in long-term memory.

why.title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory
why.found: Reviewed a wide range of studies and concluded that the real limit is three to five chunks. The famous "seven" was a rough estimate.
why.means: Plan for about four new ideas at a time, not seven.

items.title: About four
items.text: The number of new ideas a person can hold at once.

items.title: Chunks, not items
items.text: A group of related details counts as one thing.

items.title: Practice frees space
items.text: An idea that has settled in long-term memory stops taking up room.

try.text: Take a dense block of your own content. Regroup it so a newcomer meets no more than four new ideas at a time. Write down what you grouped and why.

try.title: A one-hour induction
try.text: Before: nine policies on nine slides. After: three groups (how you get paid, how you stay safe, who to ask), one short activity for each, and the detail in a handout.

items: Adding slides does not help if each slide still carries six ideas.
"Seven, plus or minus two" is the older figure. Later work puts the limit nearer four.
What counts as "new" depends on the person. A room of experts can take far more.

topics.title: Cut the load that teaches nothing
topics.theory: Cognitive load, worked examples, expertise reversal

situation.text: Your material is accurate and complete, and people still look lost. Often the content is not the problem. The way it is presented is using up the thinking space people need.

items: Cut anything that makes people work without teaching them: decoration, repetition, hunting for the right place on the page.
For newcomers, show a fully worked example before you ask them to solve one.
Put words next to the picture they describe, not on a separate slide or page.
Do not read out text that is already on the screen.
As people improve, take the support away. Help that suits a beginner slows an expert down.

why.text: Mental effort during learning comes from two places. Some is the real difficulty of the subject. Some is wasted on poor design. Only the second kind is worth cutting.

Three effects come up constantly. Beginners learn more from studying worked solutions than from solving problems unaided. Splitting related information across places forces people to hold one part while they find the other. Saying and showing the same words at once overloads people. And all of this reverses with expertise: support that helps a novice gets in the way of someone who already knows.

items.title: Cut the waste first
items.text: Remove effort that comes from the design, not the subject.

items.title: Examples before problems
items.text: Newcomers learn more from a worked solution.

items.title: Fade the help
items.text: What helps a beginner holds an expert back.

try.text: Find one resource you know is hard to follow. List what makes people work without teaching them. Redesign it, and label each fix with the effect it addresses.

items: Do not strip out the difficulty that belongs to the subject. That effort is the learning.
The different kinds of load are hard to measure separately. Use the idea as a design guide, not as a measuring tool.
In a mixed room, one level of support will be wrong for someone. Give the experienced people the harder version.

quiz.a: The effort caused by the design: decoration, repetition, hunting for the right place. Not the difficulty that belongs to the subject.

quiz.q: What helps a beginner more than solving problems unaided?

topics.title: Make practice harder in the ways that help
topics.theory: Desirable difficulties: spacing, retrieval, interleaving, generation

situation.text: The session went smoothly and everyone said it was clear. Two weeks later very little is left. Smooth is often the problem.

items: Spread practice over time. Come back to the key ideas after a gap, not only on the day.
Ask people to recall before you remind them. A short quiz with no notes beats a recap.
Once the basics are in, mix related problem types so people must work out which approach fits.
Ask for an answer before you give one, even if the answer is wrong.
Tell people why the harder practice is there. Otherwise they will resist it.

why.text: Conditions that feel harder in the moment often make learning last longer. Pulling something out of memory with effort strengthens it more than seeing it again.

Four techniques follow from this: spacing, retrieval practice, interleaving and generation. There is no single correct gap for spacing. In one large study the best gap was about a fifth of the time until the test when the test was a few weeks away, and a much smaller share when it was a year away. Longer goals need longer gaps.

why.title: Test-enhanced learning
why.found: Students either re-read a passage or tested themselves on it. After five minutes the re-readers remembered more. After two days and after a week the self-testers did, even though the re-readers had been more confident.
why.means: Swap the recap for a recall exercise, and expect it to feel worse on the day.

items.title: Space it
items.text: Practice spread over days beats one long session.

items.title: Recall it
items.text: Retrieving an idea strengthens it more than re-reading it.

items.title: Mix it
items.text: Mixed practice teaches people to tell situations apart.

try.text: Take a lesson you already teach. Mark where each of the four techniques could go, then rewrite its practice schedule.

items: Difficulty only helps people who know enough to get through it. Newcomers may need some straightforward, blocked practice first.
Interleaving helps most when the things being mixed are related and easy to confuse. The pooled studies advise caution with word lists and explanatory texts.
Learners usually rate the easier method as more effective. Their sense of it is unreliable.

topics.title: Do not trust how fluent the room looks

situation.text: You need to judge whether a session worked. The room was engaged, answers came quickly and the feedback forms are warm.

items: Do not judge a method by how fluent people look during the session.
Check again after a delay, when the easy familiarity has worn off.
Compare methods on what people can do later, not on how the session felt.
Teach learners to distrust the feeling of "I know this" that comes from re-reading.

why.text: How well people perform during a session is a poor guide to what they have learned. Methods that raise performance on the day often produce the weakest retention, and the reverse.

Memory fades without reinforcement, which is the original reason for coming back to material later. And people misjudge their own learning: easy study feels productive, effortful practice feels worse, and the truth is usually the other way round.

items.text: Fluency on the day says little about next month.

items.title: Test after a delay
items.text: The delayed check is the honest one.

items.title: Feelings mislead

try.text: Pick a course you know. Find one place where looking fluent has been taken as having learned. Design a delayed check that would show the truth.

items: The forgetting curve is an illustration, not a precise law. Do not quote exact percentages from it.
A delayed check that shows a drop is useful information, not a failure of the session.
Do not swing to making everything hard. See the topic on difficulties that help.

topics.title: Tell adults why, and start from their problems
topics.theory: Adult learning, used as a rule of thumb

situation.text: You are planning for experienced adults who did not choose to be there and want to know what is in it for them.

items: Say why the session matters to their work, in the first few minutes.
Start from a problem they recognise, not from the subject.
Ask what they already do, and build on it.
Give real choices where you can: which case, which order, which example.

why.text: The classic account of adult learning says adults are more self-directed, bring experience, care about problems more than subjects and need to know why. These are useful starting points for design.
They are rules of thumb, not laws. The evidence is mixed, and the sharp line between how adults and children learn does not fully hold.

items.title: Why first
items.text: Adults want the reason before the content.

items.title: Problems, not subjects

items.title: A rule of thumb

try.text: Rewrite the opening of one module for a specific audience. State the why, and tie it to a problem that audience really has.

items: Experience cuts both ways. People bring knowledge to build on, and misconceptions to manage.
Do not present these principles as proven. Say they are a working guide.
Choice needs structure. Too much freedom leaves newcomers lost.

topics.title: Build practice at the edge of ability

situation.text: People have done the job for years and have stopped improving. You are asked to make them better at something they already do.

items: Name one specific weakness to work on, not the whole skill.
Set the task just beyond what the person can do comfortably.
Give feedback straight away, on that weakness.
Repeat, adjust, and repeat again.
Never promise mastery from hours alone.

why.text: Experience by itself does not build expertise. Improvement comes from practice that is effortful, aimed at a weakness, pitched at the edge of ability and followed by feedback.

The "10,000 hours" figure is a popularisation, and the researcher it is credited to objected to it. A later pooling of studies found that deliberate practice explained about a quarter of the difference in performance in games, about a fifth in music and sport, and under one per cent in professions.

items.title: Aim at a weakness
items.text: General repetition keeps people where they are.

items.title: Edge of ability
items.text: Hard enough that errors happen and teach.

items.title: Hours are not enough
items.text: Twenty years can be one year repeated.

try.text: Choose a skill you are developing. Design one drill for it. Write down the weakness it targets, the level of challenge and where the feedback comes from.

items: Comfortable repetition feels like practice and is not.
Practice at the edge is tiring. Keep it short and plan recovery.
Without feedback, people practise their mistakes.

topics.title: Start from what people already know

situation.text: You teach a correct idea clearly. People nod, and go on using the wrong one they arrived with.

items: Find out what people already believe before you teach.
Build on what is right.
Name a common wrong idea and show where it fails.
Give the correct idea, then have people use it.
Check again later. Old ideas come back.

why.text: New learning is built on what people already know. What they know helps when it is accurate and gets in the way when it is not.
A wrong idea that is not addressed tends to survive the lesson. Telling people the right answer is often not enough. They need to see the old idea fail.

try.text: Before your next session, write three wrong ideas people are likely to bring. Plan how you will surface and test each.

items: Do not humiliate people for a wrong idea. Most were taught it.
Repeating a myth can strengthen it. State the fact first.
Experienced groups hold stronger wrong ideas.

topics.title: Know the main theories of learning and what each is good for
topics.theory: A map of learning theories: behaviourist, cognitive, constructivist, social, experiential

situation.text: A client asks which learning theory your course is "based on". You are not sure what the choices are.

items: Learn the five families in one line each.
For a skill that needs fluency, borrow from behaviourism: practice, feedback, reinforcement.
For understanding, borrow from cognitive theory: memory, load, recall.
For judgement, borrow from constructivism: problems and discussion.
For norms and craft, borrow from social and experiential theory: watching, doing, reflecting.

why.text: Behaviourism looks at what people do and what follows. Cognitive theory looks at memory and thinking. Constructivism says people build understanding from experience. Social theory says people learn by watching and working with others. Experiential theory says people learn by doing and reflecting.
Each explains some kinds of learning well and others badly. A working trainer uses them as tools for different jobs.

items.title: Tools for jobs
items.text: Match the theory to the kind of learning.

try.text: Take one course you know. Find one activity that fits each family. Note which family is missing.

items: Theory names are used to sell products. Ask what the method is.
Constructivist does not mean unguided. Newcomers need guidance.
This is a map. Each family has a large literature.

parts.title: Spot the myths
parts.summary: Why brain myths spread, the big ones debunked, and how to test a claim.

topics.title: Know why smart people believe brain myths

situation.text: A supplier, a colleague or your own old slides make a confident claim about "how the brain learns". It sounds scientific and you are tempted to repeat it.

items: Treat any "brain-based" claim as unproven until you have seen the source.
Trace the claim back to the finding it came from. Check what that finding really showed.
Ask who gains if you believe it.
Apply the same test to your own materials and branding.

why.text: A neuromyth is a real finding about the brain or learning that has been stretched or distorted. They spread because they are plausible and often flattering.

Two findings explain why careful people fall for them. In one experiment, adding irrelevant brain language made weak explanations more satisfying to people without neuroscience training. Experts were not taken in. In a survey of 242 teachers in the UK and the Netherlands, all of them interested in the neuroscience of learning, teachers believed about half of the myths they were shown. Those who knew more about the brain believed more of them. Interest is not protection.

items.title: A distortion, not a lie
items.text: Most myths start from something true.

items.title: Brain words persuade
items.text: Neuroscience language makes weak claims sound strong.

items.title: Interest is not immunity
items.text: Knowing more about the brain did not protect teachers.

try.text: Take one real marketing claim for "brain-based" training. Trace it back to the finding it distorts, and write one sentence on what the finding actually supports.

items: A trainer is a trusted source. When you repeat a myth, it spreads with your authority behind it.
Do not overcorrect into dismissing all neuroscience. The findings are real. The stretching is the problem.

topics.title: Drop learning styles and the other big myths

situation.text: A client asks for training that suits "visual, auditory and kinaesthetic learners", or a questionnaire to sort people by style.

items: Stop sorting people by learning style. Remove the questionnaires.
Choose the medium that suits the content: show a process, describe a principle, practise a skill.
Use more than one medium when it helps understanding, for everyone.
When someone raises a myth, name what is true in it before you correct it.

why.text: People do have preferences. What the evidence does not support is the claim that teaching someone in their preferred style improves their learning.

The same goes for several other popular ideas. We use virtually all of our brain, not a tenth. People are not left-brained or right-brained learners. Listening to Mozart does not raise intelligence in any lasting way. Learning styles persist because the idea is intuitive, flattering and gives people a tidy label.

items.title: Preference is not benefit
items.text: Liking a style does not mean learning better from it.

items.title: Match the content
items.text: Pick the medium for the subject, not for the person.

items.title: Several media, for all
items.text: Mixing media is sound. Matching to styles is not.

try.text: Audit one course or brochure for myths. Rewrite the parts that rest on them.

items: Do not shame people for believing it. Most were taught it by a trainer.
Related claims need the same care: "digital natives", fixed attention spans, and big effects from hydration or sugar.
Using several media is good practice. Say so, or people hear "pictures do not matter".

topics.title: Test any learning claim before you repeat it
topics.theory: Evaluating a claim: evidence levels, effect sizes, red flags

situation.text: A report, a vendor or a conference talk claims a method "improves learning by 40%". You have to decide whether to act on it.

items: Find out what kind of evidence it is: a story, one study, several studies, or a pooled analysis of many.
Ask "compared to what?". An effect means little without the comparison.
Look at the size of the effect, not only whether it was "significant".
Check who paid for the research and who gains from the claim.
Write down what would have to be true for the claim to hold.

why.text: Evidence comes in strengths. A single story is the weakest. One study is better. Findings repeated by others are better still, and a careful pooling of many studies is the strongest common form.

A result can be statistically significant and still too small to matter in practice. The usual warning signs are brain language with no reference, the phrase "brain-based", a claim that flatters the buyer, no comparison group, and a commercial interest that is not declared.

items.title: Compared to what?

items.title: Size matters

items: This is a way of judging, not a guarantee. Strong evidence in schools may not carry over to your workplace.

parts.title: The body matters
parts.summary: Sleep, stress and energy across a training day.

topics.title: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes

situation.text: You are planning a residential, a bootcamp or a run of full days. The temptation is to fill every hour, including the evenings.

items: Protect the nights. End early enough for a full night of sleep.
Do not run fourteen-hour days. They undo what the day built.
Start each morning by recalling yesterday before adding anything new.
Build in real breaks, and a quiet period after demanding sessions.

why.text: Memories are stabilised and connected during sleep. That is one reason practice spread over days works better than one long sitting: sleep falls between the sessions.
Too little sleep hurts at both ends. It weakens taking in new material the next day and it weakens keeping what was learned the day before.

items.title: Sleep is part of the course
Long days cost learning
items.text: The extra hours come out of retention.

try.text: Take the timetable of a real multi-day programme. Ignore the content. Mark where sleep is cut short and where there is no gap to settle, then redesign the rhythm.

items: Keep claims modest. The mechanism is real, and it is easy to inflate.
A popular book on sleep, Why We Sleep, is widely criticised for overstating its case. Lead with the research review instead.
Social evenings matter on a residential. Protect sleep without banning them.

topics.title: Take chronic stress out of the room

situation.text: People arrive tense: a restructure is under way, the session is assessed, or senior people are in the room.

items: Remove public failure. Let people try things in pairs before the whole room.

why.text: Stress that goes on for a long time gets in the way of taking in and recalling information. A learner who feels threatened is not only uncomfortable. They are less able to learn.

topics.title: Give people choice, progress and connection

situation.text: The training is mandatory and nobody wants to be there. Someone suggests prizes or a leaderboard.

items: Give meaningful choice: which case, which order, how to show what they have learned.
Set challenges people can meet, and show them their progress.
Build connection: pairs, small groups, shared problems.
Explain the value of the task before you reach for rewards.
Keep rewards for tasks that are dull but necessary.

why.text: One of the better-supported accounts of motivation says people need three things: a sense of choice, a sense of getting better, and a sense of connection to others. Design for those and people engage more willingly.

External rewards can backfire. A pooling of 128 experiments found that tangible rewards reduced people's interest in tasks they already enjoyed, while positive feedback increased it. Motivation also depends on two judgements: whether I expect to succeed, and whether I value the result. You can design for both.

try.text: Take one mandatory, unpopular topic. Reframe it so people expect to succeed and can see why it matters, without adding rewards.

items: Your job is rarely to make content fun. It is to help people see its value.
Points and badges are not harmless decoration. They change why people take part.

topics.title: Make it safe to be wrong out loud
topics.theory: Psychological safety and the error climate

situation.text: You ask a question and nobody answers. People are not short of ideas. They are working out whether it is safe to be wrong in front of this group.

items: Show your own mistakes early.
Frame activities as learning, not as judgement.
Invite people in by name and by turn, not only the confident few.
Treat a wrong answer as useful, and say why.
Build this before you ask people to take risks, not after.

why.text: Psychological safety is a shared belief that it is safe to take a risk in this group: to ask, to admit a mistake, to offer a half-formed idea. Learning depends on exactly those behaviours.

The idea grew out of a study of eight hospital units. The units with more open leaders recorded more drug errors, not fewer, and the likely reason is that people there felt able to report them. A later study of 51 teams in a manufacturing company found that psychological safety went with more learning behaviour. Safety is not the same as being nice. It is candour with respect.

Training that encourages people to make errors and learn from them has been pooled across 24 studies. It came out ahead of training that avoids errors, most of all when people later met a task they had not practised.

situation.text: On a long programme people drift away by week three. Those who leave often decided early that they could not do it, or did not belong.

why.text: Belief in your own ability to succeed is built from four things: succeeding at something real, seeing people like you succeed, being told you can by someone credible, and how you read your own nerves. The first is the strongest.

Belonging matters most to people with a reason to doubt it. In a study of US college students, a short exercise that eased doubts about fitting in raised the grades of Black students and made no difference to white students. topics.title: Have learners teach each other

situation.text: You have a cohort with mixed experience and not enough of your own time to coach everyone.

items: Have each person prepare to teach one part to a partner.

why.text: Preparing to teach, and teaching, deepens learning for the person doing the teaching. Explaining forces you to organise what you know and find the gaps.

The best-known version is peer instruction, used for ten years in introductory physics at Harvard. Students answer a question alone, discuss it with a neighbour, then answer again. The authors report better grasp of the concepts and better problem solving than before they introduced it.

Peer feedback helps when it is structured and is unreliable when it is not. The outline also says that groups who learn together finish at higher rates than people studying alone. The source for that has not been found yet.

situation.text: A manager says "we need training on X". Before you design anything, find out whether training can fix it.

why.text: Poor performance has many causes, and lack of skill is only one. People may not know what is expected, may lack the tools, may get no feedback, or may be rewarded for doing something else.

situation.text: The course aims say people will "understand" and "be aware of". Nobody can tell whether it worked.

items: Start from what people must be able to do at the end.

why.text: Designing backwards means choosing the capability first, then the assessment, then the teaching. Objectives, activities and assessment must point at the same target. When they do not, the course is misaligned, which is the commonest design fault.
Bloom's taxonomy is a useful ladder for pitching the level of thinking. Use it as a guide, not a strict hierarchy.

items: Check where people start before you teach.
Add short, low-stakes checks during the course.

why.text: Assessment has three purposes: to find the starting point, to guide learning while it happens, and to judge it at the end. The middle one is among the strongest levers on learning.

topics.title: Judge every slide by what it asks of the learner

situation.text: The slide looks professional and the room is still lost. Looking good and teaching well are different things.

items: For each slide, ask what the learner has to do with it.
Help them pick out what matters.
Help them organise it.
Help them connect it to what they know.
Remove whatever does none of these.

why.text: The leading theory of learning from words and pictures rests on three ideas. People take in pictures and words through separate channels. Each channel holds little. Learning needs active work by the learner.
Design either supports that work or gets in its way. The principles shift with expertise, as with cognitive load.
